issues.label: Standard of review for RAD's interpretation and application of s. 110(4) IRPA
Reasonableness of RAD's interpretation of s. 110(4) IRPA (use of Raza test)
Reasonableness of RAD's application of s. 110(4) IRPA to the facts (admissibility of new evidence)

result.overall: The Court granted Mr. Singh's application for judicial review, finding the RAD's interpretation and application of s. 110(4) IRPA unreasonable, particularly in its strict use of the Raza test and its expectations regarding the applicant's ability to present new evidence. The matter was remitted for redetermination and two questions were certified.

themes.name: Standard of Review for RAD Decisions
themes.summary: The Court addresses the appropriate standard of review for the RAD's interpretation and application of s. 110(4) IRPA, concluding it is reasonableness, not correctness.

themes.name: Interpretation of s. 110(4) IRPA and Use of Raza Test
themes.summary: The Court considers whether the RAD reasonably interpreted s. 110(4) by strictly applying the Raza test, ultimately finding this approach unreasonable given the RAD's appellate role.

themes.name: Admissibility of New Evidence Before the RAD
themes.summary: The Court examines whether the RAD reasonably applied s. 110(4) to the facts, especially regarding the applicant's ability to present new evidence and the expectations placed on him.

themes.name: Procedural Fairness and Access to a Full Appeal
themes.summary: The Court discusses the importance of a flexible approach to admitting new evidence to ensure claimants have access to a full fact-based appeal before the RAD.

arguments.quote: the RAD failed to admit a document that not only goes to the core of his story, but also to the RPD’s finding of credibility which consequently, gravely prejudices his claim.
arguments.claim: The RAD erred by not admitting the 2002 diploma, which was central to both his narrative and the RPD's credibility finding, causing grave prejudice.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the RAD's refusal to admit the evidence unreasonable and prejudicial.

arguments.quote: the RAD failed to properly apply Raza, as this “new evidence” satisfies the Raza test insofar that the document: (a) is credible; (b) is pertinent; (c) is “new” in that it can refute a factual conclusion drawn by the RPD; (d) is of substantial character; and (e) was not raised before the board through no fault of the applicant.
arguments.claim: The RAD misapplied the Raza test because the diploma met all its criteria and was not presented due to no fault of the applicant.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court agreed the evidence should have been admitted under a proper application of s. 110(4).

arguments.quote: The RAD could not have reasonably expected that it be produced by the applicant at the time of the RPD hearing.
arguments.claim: It was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to have produced the diploma at the RPD hearing.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the RAD's expectation unreasonable given the circumstances.

arguments.quote: the RAD failed to give sufficient weight to the following factors: 1. The document was of critical probative value to the applicant’s claim because it proved that he attended school with Bhupinder Singh at that time and that he was not lying about this fact; 2. Although the document was initially seized by the CBSA, the RPD did not believe this part of the applicant’s testimony when in fact it was true (i.e. this demonstrates that the applicant was not lying); and 3. The RAD recognized that the failure to produce the document was the fault of the lawyer yet nonetheless it blamed the applicant, whose case was entirely in the hands of his lawyer(s), and who likely did not know what documents may have been missing from his file or that the document in question was of such critical importance to his claim.
arguments.claim: The RAD failed to give sufficient weight to the diploma's probative value, the CBSA's seizure of the document, and the fact that the applicant's lawyer was at fault for its non-production.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court agreed these factors were not reasonably considered by the RAD.

arguments.quote: the RAD used the proper test by interpreting subsection 110(4) of the Act in light of similar wording in paragraph 113(a); an interpretation of the latter can assist this Court in interpreting the former.
arguments.claim: The RAD properly interpreted s. 110(4) by applying the Raza test, as the wording is similar to s. 113(a).
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the RAD's strict application of Raza unreasonable given the RAD's appellate function.

arguments.quote: The applicant was required to establish that he could not have reasonably been expected to provide the newly submitted documents at his RPD hearing. The respondent maintains the RAD did not err in finding that he failed to do so.
arguments.claim: The RAD reasonably found the applicant could have produced the diploma at the RPD hearing and did not err in refusing it.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the applicant could not reasonably have been expected to provide the document at the RPD hearing.

arguments.quote: the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD is within the tribunal’s expertise and does not involve a question of central importance to the legal system as a whole or any other special circumstances that would require review on a correctness standard.
arguments.claim: The standard of review for the RAD's interpretation of s. 110(4) is reasonableness, not correctness.

arguments.quote: the RAD owes the RPD deference and that it should review the RPD decision applying the reasonableness standard. Respectfully, I do not agree.
arguments.claim: The RAD should not owe deference to the RPD or apply a reasonableness standard to its review of RPD decisions.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court agreed the RAD should not defer to the RPD in this way.

holdings.quote: Therefore, I am of the view that both the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act (as a question of law that is not of general importance to the legal system as a whole and outside the expertise of the RAD) and its application to the facts of this case (as a question of mixed fact and law) are to be reviewed on the reasonableness standard.
holdings.statement: The standard of review for both the RAD's interpretation and application of s. 110(4) IRPA is reasonableness.

holdings.quote: In sum, I am of the view that it was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza test in interpreting subsection 110(4) of the Act all the while failing to appreciate that its role is quite different from that of a PRRA officer.
holdings.statement: It was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza test to s. 110(4) without considering its distinct appellate role.

holdings.quote: The applicant’s request to file this new evidence fell squarely, in my view, within the scope of subsection 110(4) of the Act and it met its explicit criteria.
holdings.statement: The applicant's request to file the new evidence met the criteria of s. 110(4) and should have been admitted.

holdings.quote: For these reasons, I find that both the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act and its application to the facts before it are unreasonable such that the application for judicial review should be granted and the above questions certified.
holdings.statement: The application for judicial review is granted, the RAD decision is set aside and remitted, and two questions are certified.

rebuttals.quote: it was not reasonable for the RAD to conclude that the applicant should have brought the documentary evidence before the RPD. The document was not in his possession, and he mistakenly believed that CBSA still had it, based on the fact that the agency had seized it from him initially.
rebuttals.point: The RAD reasonably found the applicant could have produced the diploma at the RPD hearing.
rebuttals.court_answer: The Court found it was unreasonable to expect the applicant to have produced the document, given the circumstances.

rebuttals.quote: it was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to file a complaint against his former lawyer as a prerequisite for filing the new evidence before the RAD.
rebuttals.point: The applicant should have filed a complaint against his former lawyer to explain the late production of the document.
rebuttals.court_answer: The Court found it unreasonable to require the applicant to know or pursue a complaint procedure against his lawyer.

authorities.quote: the respondent argues that the RAD’s determination of the appropriate analysis that is to be conducted in assessing the admissibility of new evidence should be subject to the reasonableness standard, as it involves a tribunal considering and applying its home statute: while errors of law are generally governed by a correctness standard. “ Dunsmuir [v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9] (at para. 54), says that if the interpretation of the home statute or a closely related statute by an expert decision maker is reasonable, there is no error of law justifying intervention ” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 44).
authorities.authority: Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9; Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12
authorities.why: Cited for the principle that reasonableness is the standard for tribunal interpretations of their home statute.

authorities.quote: The respondent further cites Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission) v Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11 at para 167, interpreting Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner) v Alberta Teachers’ Association, [2011] 3 SCR 654 [Alberta Teachers] at para 30 on the exceptions where correctness will apply:
authorities.authority: Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission) v Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11; Alberta Teachers’ Association, [2011] 3 SCR 654
authorities.why: Cited for the exceptions to the reasonableness standard.

authorities.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada has since not identified a case that raised a “question of central importance to the legal system as a whole.” Moreover, since Alberta Teachers, the Supreme Court of Canada has reiterated its strict limitations to the use of the exceptions to the reasonableness standard. In McLean v British Columbia (Securities Commission), 2013 SCC 67, the Court found that deference is owed to provincial securities’ regulators interpretation of statute of limitation provisions, despite it being a “technical” question, rather than a “bureaucratic” one.
authorities.authority: McLean v British Columbia (Securities Commission), 2013 SCC 67
authorities.why: Cited to reinforce the strict limits on exceptions to reasonableness review.

authorities.quote: the RAD applied the criteria emanating from Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 [Raza] at para 13, and evaluated the credibility, the relevance, the newness, and the materiality of the evidence in order to decide on its admissibility.
authorities.authority: Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385
authorities.why: The Court found the Raza test should not be strictly applied to RAD appeals due to the RAD's different role.

left_open.quote: As indicated above, I am of the view that said question is not determinative of the present case and that it would not be determinative of an appeal.
left_open.issue: Whether the RAD owes deference to RPD findings of fact and of mixed fact and law.
left_open.reason: The Court found this question not determinative of the present case.
